newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Donors still wait for Ivorian cocoa auction data.
newsitem.headline: Donors still wait for Ivorian cocoa auction data.

text.p: International donors are still waiting for Ivory Coast to supply cocoa auction trading data before releasing a final instalment of a $150 million farm loan, donor representatives say.
"The loan review comes up in June. One condition of the CASA (Agricultural Sector Adjustment Credit) is that the auction system is seen to be working," one said.

Ivory Coast's Caistab cocoa marketing board switched trading from a closed-door system to a donor-sponsored auction system in April 1996 to boost efficiency and transparency in export contract allocation.
Exporters asked for three rule changes in late 1996 saying they wanted to stop overbidding and concentration of awarded contracts in a few hands.
Donors have said they cannot decide until the Caistab releases auction trade data. Ivorian Agriculture Minister Lambert Kouassi Konan confirmed in February that data was being witheld.
"If the World Bank studies the trade data and sees that proposed changes are needed then loan conditions can quickly be met," one representative said.
Donor representatives say they only need to see trends.
"We need to see overall prices and quantities traded so far," said one. "We do not want details on particular exporters and what they have paid. It is not confidential data that is needed."
Donors have already agreed to two of the three proposed rule changes.
The first rule change concerns quantities on offer to Ivory Coast-based exporters, and international traders.
Current rules allow 85 percent of cocoa contracts to be sold to exporters in each session, with 15 percent reserved by the Caistab for direct sale to foreign traders.
A new rule would mean that local exporters would be allowed to buy all contracts of cocoa put on sale by the Caistab on a particular day -- if they bid the highest prices.
At present, if foreign traders bid less than exporters the 15 percent reserved for them is removed from auction for later sale.
Trade sources say that the Caistab's main contract with a foreign trader is due to end in late 1997.
The second rule change concerns prices bid to win contracts.
Under exisiting rules, the Caistab does not announce in advance how much cocoa is up for each daily auction.
An exporter happening to bid for the whole amount at the highest price wins all 85 percent allocated to exporters -- paying his bid price.
Contracts are awarded at the second highest price if no exporter bids for the whole amount. Everyone is eligible to buy at that price and contacts are allocated pro-rata based on amounts requested.
A proposed rule change would mean the second-highest-price rule would be scrapped.
Exporters would still share out the amount on offer, but each would pay for his share at the price he had offered. Two exporters could win the same amounts but pay different prices.
Such a change could encourage exporters to form a cartel and bid at uniformly low prices but supporters of the idea say competition for contracts would make this unlikely.
"It is open to that but it would probably not happen as exporters are more interested in winning contracts on offer than divided contracts, albeit at a lower price," one said.
Trade sources say the Caistab opposes the third proposed rule change.
The GEPEX exporters trade body is proposing an alternative system of pricing which would allow all bidders at the five highest levels on any particular day to be awarded contracts.
Progress talks between donors, exporters and government officials have been pencilled in for April.
((-- Matthew Bunce, Abidjan newsroom + 225 21 90 90))
